processing: Light to medium oxidation with vigorous shaking, semi-ball-rolled or strip-rolled, and a light to medium roast; a strongly aromatic, high-polyphenol leaf that is also made into black tea.
harvest_season: Spring (April) and autumn (October), with summer pickings in the warm lowland gardens; spring and autumn are the quality harvests.
appearance_dry: Tight, slightly curved, dark olive-green to brown semi-rolled strips with a strong floral-fruity smell.
appearance_wet: Large, long, thick leaves, yellow-green with red edges.
taste_profile: An intense, almost dancong-like floral and fruit aroma, a strong, slightly bitter body that turns to a long sweetness, and a clean, cooling finish.

brewing.notes: Rinse once and keep the early steeps very short; the leaf is strong and goes bitter fast. Brewed with a light hand it is fragrant and sweet, brewed heavy it is bracing. A gaiwan shows the aroma best.

vintage_note: Sold by season, spring and autumn of the current year, mostly within Fujian and Guangdong; green-style lots are best within the year kept cool, roasted lots keep two to three years. It is rarely aged and the year is usually stated on the pack.
description:
Ba Xian, Eight Immortals, from Zhao'an county on Fujian's border with Guangdong is a strong, perfumed oolong that tastes like a bridge between the Minnan and the Phoenix dancong traditions, which makes geographical sense: Zhao'an is the last county in Fujian before Chaozhou. It should not be confused with the Phoenix dancong strain called Ba Xian, a different plant that happens to share the name.

The cultivar is a twentieth-century selection. One report traces it to wild tea around Ding'an village in Xiuzhuan, in the north of the county, with local tea specialists raising the mother plants in the 1960s; it was approved as a national cultivar in 1994. It is noted for a high polyphenol content, which is why it brews strong and slightly bitter and why it is also used for black tea.

As oolong it is withered and shaken hard to build aroma, oxidised to a light or medium level, rolled into curled strips or semi-balls and roasted lightly to moderately. The cup is golden, the aroma is big, floral and fruity in a way that recalls a Mi Lan Xiang dancong, and the body is firm with a bitterness that resolves into a long sweetness, then a cooling finish.

Brew it in a gaiwan with boiling water and genuinely short steeps, five to ten seconds at first; it has a lot to give and gives it quickly, and a careless long steep turns it harsh. Seven infusions is normal, and it is a good tea for drinkers who find Tieguanyin too soft.

It is sold by season, spring and autumn, mostly within southern Fujian and in Chaozhou, and only a few specialist sellers carry it abroad. Buy from someone who states the season and the roast level, drink green lots within the year, and if you enjoy it, the Phoenix dancongs over the provincial border are the obvious next direction.
sources_note: The 1960s breeding in Zhao'an (usually credited to Zheng Zhaoqin, 1965) and the 1994 national registration follow Chinese cultivar records; the exact parentage is given inconsistently in sources, so none is stated.
history:
Zhao'an, on the Fujian side of the Guangdong border, claims close to 400 years of tea growing, but Ba Xian as a cultivar is modern. One report traces it to wild tea around Ding'an village in Xiuzhuan, with local tea specialists raising the mother plants in the 1960s at the foot of Baxian mountain in Baiyang.

In 1994 the national tea cultivar committee approved it as a national variety, reported as the first newly bred oolong variety to reach that level since 1949. The county now holds about 95 percent of the country's plantings, and Ba Xian covers more than 80 percent of its tea area, according to a 2022 report.
